_note: Narration script for the paramedic Asthma or COPD? module (CPG-113-P/ICP, CPG-115-P/ICP, CTL-049, CPPRO-014). Lee voice on eleven_v4, planned as two takes (scenes 1-4 and 5-8). The prompt sent to ElevenLabs starts with the [calmly] tag and spells EOC, ICP, CPAP as said, SpO2 as S P O 2, mL as mils; captions use the text here.

lines.head: The patient
sentences: She has COPD, and she's on home oxygen.
Tonight she's wheezing, and she can't finish a sentence.

lines.head: Grade the asthma
sentences: So is being visibly breathless, or an SpO2 of 90 to 94.

lines.head: Oxygen
sentences: For severe asthma, it's high-flow oxygen.
For COPD, you titrate to 88 to 92 percent.
Too much oxygen can tip a COPD patient into respiratory failure.
But the COPD guideline says keep 88 to 92, even if the CO2 rises.

lines.head: The same in both
sentences: Some treatment is the same in both.
Prednisolone, or for the ICP, IV hydrocortisone 250 milligrams.
Only if there have been no steroids in the past 24 hours.

lines.head: Magnesium and adrenaline
sentences: The ICP gives 10 millimoles over 20 minutes.
By syringe driver, that's 50 mL at 150 an hour.
The asthma guideline says consider it, if it's life-threatening.
The COPD guideline says there's no evidence for it.

lines.head: CPAP
sentences: CPAP is COPD only, and it's ICP scope.
Then it's CPAP at 5 centimetres of water.
Give the nebs inline, with salbutamol 15 milligrams.
Not if you suspect a pneumothorax.
And take it off if the systolic drops below 100.

lines.head: Know your source
sentences: So, for every drug you give, know which guideline it came from.
Write it down, and hand it over.
And if you're not sure, consult.
